sections.html: The large-growing, magnificent Panaque bathyphilus is very variable in coloration. Specimens 16-20 cm long are about half grown, as the maximum length given for P. bathyphilus is about 60 cm.
P. bathyphilus occurs in Peru (surroundings of Tingo Maria).
Peru: Solimões River (in the Amazon River drainage).
A deep river channel species, which accounts for the lack of an iris operculum. The deeper they reside, the less pigmentation on the body.
These large fish should only be kept in large aquariums with strong filtration.
This species is a bit robust in an aquarium set-up, so it needs plenty of hiding places, plenty of water changes due to its wood-eating habits, and powerful filtration. It needs a spacious aquarium.

Like all Panaque, P. bathyphilus is predominantly a wood eater. The amount of feces produced by this nutrient-poor diet is enormous, which is another reason why large tanks with strong filtration are necessary.
All Panaques and also the Panaqolus genera are wood eaters, so wood is needed in an aquarium set-up. Also feed vegetable foods such as cucumber, courgette (zucchini) and sinking tablets.
Among themselves Panaque are not quite without aggression and can become quite rough. However, L90 is considered one of the more tolerant species in this regard.

This species was first published in the German magazine DATZ in January 1992 as the L-number 90.

Description: The differences between the Panaqolus and the Panaque genera is that the latter has an oval shaped mouth and the jaws have very large spatulate teeth with a single cusp, arranged in a V form, while Panaqolus have a small number of spatulate teeth and are also a smaller genus.

Colouration: Juveniles of P. bathyphilus have a white caudal fin, but it becomes a little darker on the posterior as it matures.

Etymology: The specific name bathyphilus means deep-loving, from bathýs, deep, and phílos, friend or fond of, referring to its deep-river-channel habitat.

IUCN Red List: Despite the little information available on this species, it has no apparent threats and a large range. Therefore, it is assessed as Least Concern (LC) (IUCN 2023).

Lujan, NK and CC Chamon (2008) Two new species of Loricariidae (Teleostei: Siluriformes) from main channels of the upper and middle Amazon Basin, with discussion of deep water specialization in loricariids. Ichthyological Exploration of Freshwaters 19: 271–282.
